text: When mankind began to multiply on the face of the earth, and daughters were born to them,

versions.text: When human beings began to multiply on the face of the earth, and daughters were born to them,
versions.explanation: The same Hebrew word ha'adam is rendered 'human beings' here but 'men' in verses 2 and 4 and 'man' in verse 5. Consistent wording preserves the deliberate contrast between 'sons of God' and 'daughters of mankind' and reads more smoothly aloud across the paragraph.

text: the sons of God saw that the daughters of mankind were beautiful, and they took as wives any of them they chose.

versions.text: the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives any they chose.
versions.explanation: Verse 1 was deliberately revised to render ha'adam as 'mankind' for consistency across the paragraph, but verse 2 still has 'men.' Matching the wording preserves the intended contrast between 'sons of God' and 'daughters of mankind.' Adding 'of them' also reflects mikkol asher bacharu ('from all whom they chose') and reads more smoothly aloud.

text: Then the LORD said, "My Spirit shall not contend* with man forever, for he is flesh. His days shall be a hundred and twenty years." [*Footnote: The meaning of the Hebrew verb is uncertain; it may also mean 'remain in' or 'abide with.']

versions.text: Then the LORD said, "My Spirit shall not contend with man forever, for he is flesh. His days shall be a hundred and twenty years."
versions.explanation: The verb yadon occurs only here and its sense is genuinely disputed ('contend with,' 'abide in,' 'remain with'). A short footnote alerts the reader without disturbing the main text, which reads well as it stands.

text: The Nephilim* were on the earth in those days—and afterward as well—when the sons of God went in to the daughters of mankind and they bore them children. These were the mighty men of old, men of renown. [*Footnote: The meaning of the Hebrew word Nephilim is uncertain; it is often understood as referring to giants.]

versions.text: The Nephilim were on the earth in those days—and afterward as well—when the sons of God went in to the daughters of men and they bore them children. These were the mighty men of old, men of renown.
versions.explanation: 'Nephilim' is left untranslated and will be opaque to hearers; a brief footnote on the uncertain meaning helps the reader. The wording 'daughters of mankind' also brings this verse into line with the consistency already established in verse 1.

text: The LORD saw how great the wickedness of mankind had become on the earth, and that every inclination of the thoughts of the human heart was nothing but evil all the time.

versions.text: The LORD saw how great the wickedness of man had become on the earth, and that every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was nothing but evil all the time.
versions.explanation: Verses 1, 2 and 4 were deliberately revised to render ha'adam as 'mankind' for consistency across the paragraph, but verse 5 still reads 'man,' and the following 'his heart' then has no clear antecedent for a hearer. Matching the established wording keeps the section consistent and clarifies the pronoun when read aloud.

text: And the LORD regretted that he had made mankind on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart.

versions.text: And the LORD regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart.
versions.explanation: For consistency with the rendering of ha'adam as 'mankind' established in the surrounding verses; it also avoids the ambiguity of 'man' (male) immediately before 'it grieved him.'

text: So the LORD said, "I will wipe from the face of the earth the human race I have created—from man to animals, to creatures that crawl and birds of the sky—for I regret that I made them."

versions.text: So the LORD said, "I will wipe from the face of the earth the human race I have created—man and animals, creatures that crawl and birds of the sky—for I regret that I made them."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew uses the 'from X to Y' idiom (me'adam ad behemah) to express the whole sweep of creation. 'Man and animals' flattens this range; restoring 'from... to...' keeps the cumulative rhythm of the list.

text: But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.
This is the account of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time, and he walked with God.
Noah had three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
Now the earth was corrupt in God's sight, and the earth was filled with violence.

versions.text: Now the earth was corrupt in God's sight and full of violence.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has two parallel clauses, each beginning with 'the earth,' a repetition that gives the verse its solemn weight and prepares for the same wording in verse 13 ('the earth is filled with violence'). Compressing it into 'and full of violence' loses the parallelism and the oral cadence.

text: God saw the earth, and behold, it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted its way on the earth.

versions.text: God saw how corrupt the earth had become, for all flesh had corrupted its way on the earth.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew presents the scene through God's eyes with the vivid 'and behold' (wehinneh), which the current rendering removes. Restoring it keeps the dramatic pause that works well when read aloud.

text: So God said to Noah, "The end of all flesh has come before me, for the earth is filled with violence because of them. And behold, I am about to destroy them, along with the earth.

versions.text: So God said to Noah, "I have decided to put an end to all flesh, for the earth is filled with violence because of them. Now I am going to destroy them along with the earth.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew is a declaration ('the end of all flesh has come before me'), not a statement of decision. The interpretive rendering adds 'I have decided,' which is not in the text, and loses the vivid imagery of the end arriving before God.

versions.text: So God said to Noah, "The end of all flesh has come before me, for the earth is filled with violence because of them. Now I am going to destroy them along with the earth.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew hinneni plus participle is the same attention-drawing particle (hinneh) that was deliberately restored as 'behold' in the preceding verse; rendering it as a bare 'Now' loses that echo. 'I am about to destroy' also conveys the imminence of the participle more precisely than 'I am going to destroy,' and the added comma gives the reader a natural breath before the final clause when read aloud.

text: Make yourself an ark of cypress wood;* make rooms in it and coat it with pitch inside and out. [*Footnote: Hebrew gopher wood; the exact kind of tree is unknown.]

versions.text: Make yourself an ark of cypress wood; make rooms in it and coat it with pitch inside and out.
versions.explanation: 'Cypress' is a reasonable guess, but the Hebrew word gopher occurs only here and its meaning is uncertain. A brief footnote would help the reader.

text: This is how you are to build it: the ark is to be three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.

Make a roof for the ark,* finishing it to a cubit from the top, and put a door in the side of the ark. Build it with lower, middle, and upper decks. [*Footnote: The Hebrew word rendered 'roof' is uncertain; it may mean an opening for light.]

versions.text: Make a roof for the ark, leaving a cubit's opening below it, and put a door in the side of the ark. Build it with lower, middle, and upper decks.
versions.explanation: 'Leaving a cubit's opening below it' is confusing when read aloud and goes beyond the Hebrew, which says 'to a cubit you shall finish it from above.' A footnote could note that the meaning of tsohar (roof/light opening) is uncertain.

versions.text: Make a roof for the ark, finishing it to a cubit from the top, and put a door in the side of the ark. Build it with lower, middle, and upper decks.
versions.explanation: The revision note for this verse observed that a footnote would help, but none was added. The meaning of tsohar is genuinely disputed (roof, or light opening), and a brief note serves the reader without disturbing the improved main text.

text: As for me, I am about to bring the floodwaters on the earth, to destroy all flesh under the heavens that has the breath of life in it. Everything on the earth will perish.

versions.text: I am going to bring a flood of waters on the earth, to destroy all flesh under the heavens that has the breath of life in it. Everything on the earth will perish.
versions.explanation: The doubled emphatic 'And I—behold, I' (wa'ani hineni) is strongly emphatic in Hebrew and is flattened here. Recovering the emphasis strengthens the oral rhythm and the contrast with Noah in verse 18.

text: But I will establish my covenant with you, and you will enter the ark—you and your sons and your wife and your sons' wives with you.
You are to bring into the ark two of every living creature, of all flesh, to keep them alive with you—male and female.
Birds of every kind, animals of every kind, and creatures that crawl on the ground of every kind—two of each will come to you to be kept alive.
And you—take for yourself every kind of food that is eaten, and gather it in; it will be food for you and for them."

versions.text: Take with you every kind of food that is eaten and store it away, to serve as food for you and for them."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew opens with the emphatic pronoun וְאַתָּה ('and you'), which parallels the emphatic 'As for me' of verse 17 and marks the shift from God's action to Noah's task. The current rendering flattens this contrast. Also, 'gather it to yourself/in' is closer to וְאָסַפְתָּ אֵלֶיךָ than 'store it away.'

text: Noah did all that God had commanded him; yes, so he did.

versions.text: Noah did everything just as God commanded him.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew deliberately repeats the verb ('Noah did... so he did'), a solemn closing formula. Preserving the repetition gives the verse a fuller cadence for oral reading and reflects the emphasis of the original.

versions.text: Noah did all of it; just as God had commanded him, so he did.
versions.explanation: In the Hebrew, the phrase 'according to all that' (כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר) belongs directly with the command, not as a separate object ('all of it') of the first verb. The suggested wording keeps the deliberate repetition of the verb that the revision intentionally preserved, while joining 'all' to what God commanded and giving a smoother cadence for oral reading.
